choices.text: Reserve a pay-later compact rental.
Prebook rideshares for each leg.
Use transit downtown and rideshares.
Use taxis for each offsite leg.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The prompt omits exact fares, traffic, and ride availability, so rideshare, taxi, and rental plans are all plausible. The repeated prior no-car trips make the no-rental distractors especially tempting unless the full pattern is used.
probes.label_rationale: The Columbus facts match prior car-justified cases: early suburban client mornings and parking uncertainty in Cary, and logistics-driven rentals for Colorado and St. Pete. The no-car choices in Minneapolis, Phoenix, and Cleveland were tied to fixed urban or campus patterns, not a stable rule.
probes.query: For a fresh work trip to Columbus, I land Monday afternoon, stay downtown, and have two early mornings at a client office in Dublin. Visitor parking is available, and I am carrying sample binders. Pick the ground plan.

choices.text: Skip the rental and use rideshare with the booster.
Skip the rental and use transit plus rideshare.
Book a pay-later midsize rental.
Skip the rental and use taxis for longer legs.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Little Italy makes a no-car plan believable, and several prior urban trips used rideshare or walking. The broader record is needed to avoid turning those cases into a no-rental habit.
probes.label_rationale: Groceries, family movement, and booster logistics line up with the St. Pete change to a cancellable car and the Colorado family rental, while urban no-car decisions were conditional on easier fixed-site logistics. The current trip is not a simple downtown-only stay.
probes.query: For a new family weekend in San Diego, we are staying in Little Italy, planning a grocery stop after arrival, visiting La Jolla one morning, and bringing our travel booster. Pick the ground plan.

choices.text: Take the airport shuttle and local rideshares.
Reserve a pay-later compact rental.
Use rideshares for every leg.
Use shuttles and taxis in town.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Santa Fe shuttles and rideshares make the no-car choices credible on the prompt alone. The full prior pattern is needed to select the rental without applying an overbroad no-rental assumption.
probes.label_rationale: Flying into a different city, adding an offsite morning, and needing groceries are the kinds of current-trip logistics that supported rentals or cancellable rentals in Colorado, Cary, and St. Pete. The no-car cases stayed no-car because the sites were urban, fixed, or rideshare-reliable.
probes.query: For a fresh Santa Fe trip, I fly into ABQ, sleep in Santa Fe, have one museum day and one morning meeting outside town, and need an arrival grocery run. Pick the ground plan.

choices.text: Take Link light rail to Westlake.
Use rideshare straight to the hotel.
Take a taxi straight to the hotel.
Prebook a private sedan transfer.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Rail, rideshare, and taxi are all ordinary SEA-to-downtown choices. The many prior rideshare recommendations make the rideshare distractors plausible unless the conditional nature of those episodes is recognized.
probes.gold_action: Take Link light rail to Westlake.
probes.label_rationale: A midday solo arrival with normal luggage and a hotel directly on rail matches the Denver A Line reasoning. Prior rideshare choices in Chicago, Philadelphia, Minneapolis, D.C., and Boston were based on luggage, weather, traffic, child travel, or short-hop convenience, not a stable rideshare-first rule.
probes.query: For a fresh solo trip to Seattle, I arrive midday at SEA with a carry-on, and the hotel is by Westlake Station. Pick the arrival transfer.

choices.text: Use rideshare to the hotel.
Take a taxi to the hotel.
Prebook a car service to the hotel.
Take MAX Red Line downtown.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The prompt gives no fare, surge, or travel-time advantage, so rideshare and taxi remain reasonable. The gold depends on rejecting the apparent rideshare pattern and applying the direct-rail facts.
probes.label_rationale: The Portland facts resemble the Denver Union Station case: normal luggage, midday timing, and a direct rail-connected hotel. Rideshare was previously chosen only when current friction favored it, such as luggage at ORD, traffic at PHL, weather at MSP, short DCA access, or child logistics at BOS.
probes.query: For a fresh Portland work trip, I land at PDX midday with one roller bag, and the hotel is beside Pioneer Square. Pick the arrival transfer.

choices.text: Use rideshare to the hotel.
Take BART to Powell Street.
Take a taxi to the hotel.
Prebook a private transfer.

probes.difficulty_rationale: SFO arrivals can reasonably use BART, taxi, or rideshare, and the query does not supply prices or travel times. The hard part is not letting prior rideshare-heavy episodes become a fixed transfer rule.
probes.label_rationale: The direct station access and normal luggage point to rail, as in Denver. The prior rideshare and taxi choices were context-specific responses to bags, child travel, weather, traffic, or short city transfers, so they should not override this rail-friendly setup.
probes.query: For a fresh San Francisco work-and-museum weekend, I land at SFO before lunch with normal luggage, and the hotel is near Powell Street Station. Pick the arrival transfer.

choices.text: Fly into RIC for the closer airport.
Fly into PHF for the closest airport.
Fly into RIC and skip farther airports.
Fly into ORF and use the planned car.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Closer RIC or PHF and farther ORF are both defensible without exact savings or drive times. The tempting error is to apply the repeated convenience choices as a fixed closest-airport rule.
probes.gold_action: Fly into ORF and use the planned car.
probes.label_rationale: Prior trips favored convenient airports only when alternate savings and ground friction did not clear the threshold. The St. Pete and New York cases show that closer airports can lose to better current schedule or fare logic, and the planned car reduces the ground penalty here.
probes.query: For a fresh family trip to Williamsburg, the itinerary already includes a rental car for Jamestown and Yorktown. RIC and PHF are closer, while ORF has the nonstop that fits school hours and lower family airfare. Pick the airport plan.

choices.text: Fly into MRY because it is closest.
Fly into SJC and keep the rental car.
Fly into MRY and pay for convenience.
Fly into SFO as the Bay Area gateway.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The prompt does not give exact fare savings or transfer time, so MRY convenience remains plausible. The full pattern is needed to reject a fixed closest-airport preference.
probes.gold_action: Fly into SJC and keep the rental car.
probes.label_rationale: The record supports airport selection by current route quality, fare, ground cost, trip length, and traveler friction. Since a car is already planned and SJC improves timing and airfare, this is like choosing Tampa over Sarasota when the current schedule and price math favored it.
probes.query: For a fresh Monterey/Carmel weekend, a rental car is already in the plan for coast stops. MRY is closest, while SJC has the better-timed nonstop and lower airfare for the group. Pick the airport plan.

choices.text: Fly into AVL because it is closest.
Fly into AVL and pay for convenience.
Fly into CLT and use the planned car.
Fly into GSP as the regional alternate.

probes.difficulty_rationale: AVL is naturally attractive as the closest airport, and the prompt avoids exact drive and fare numbers. That makes the closer-airport distractors credible unless the broader threshold pattern is applied.
probes.gold_action: Fly into CLT and use the planned car.
probes.label_rationale: The user has used convenience thresholds rather than airport loyalty: DCA, SAT, BOS, LGA, and TPA decisions all turned on present savings, schedules, and ground friction. With a planned car and better nonstop timing, CLT beats the closer-airport assumption here.
probes.query: For a fresh Asheville/Blue Ridge trip, the itinerary already has a car for mountain drives. AVL is closest, while CLT has the nonstop that fits the work calendar and lower airfare. Pick the airport plan.

choices.text: Pack carry-on only for everyone.
Check one bag and carry on essentials.
Use personal items and no checked bag.
Carry on the booster and skip checked bags.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Short family trips have sometimes gone without checked bags, and carry-on-only work trips are prominent. The prompt leaves airline rules and exact packing volume unstated, making the carry-on distractors plausible.
probes.gold_action: Check one bag and carry on essentials.
probes.label_rationale: Prior family trips included a checked bag for D.C., San Antonio, and St. Pete, especially when timing, a booster, or gear mattered. Carry-on-only appeared on specific solo or lighter trips, so the family winter gear points to one checked bag now.
probes.query: For a fresh five-day family trip to Park City, we have winter layers, kid gear, and a booster. Pick the baggage plan.

choices.text: Pack carry-on only for everyone.
Use garment bags and no checked bag.
Carry on the booster and skip checked bags.
Check one shared bag and carry valuables.

probes.difficulty_rationale: A wedding weekend can still be packed carry-on-only, and the prior record contains several no-checked-bag statements. The complete pattern is needed to avoid treating carry-on as a stable personal rule.
probes.gold_action: Check one shared bag and carry valuables.
probes.label_rationale: The current mix of family travel, dress clothes, beach items, and a booster fits the checked-bag family cases in D.C., San Antonio, and St. Pete. The prior carry-on examples were trip-specific and should not control this bulkier weekend.
probes.query: For a fresh wedding weekend in Charleston with family, we have dress clothes, beach clothes, and the travel booster. Pick the baggage plan.

choices.text: Check one bag and carry the laptop.
Pack everything in a carry-on roller.
Use a personal item and no checked bag.
Ship nothing and stay carry-on only.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Because the trip is solo and work-related, the carry-on distractors are strongly tempting. The prompt omits airline bag fees and exact material size, so prior context is needed to choose checked baggage.
probes.gold_action: Check one bag and carry the laptop.
probes.label_rationale: Solo work trips often used carry-on-only, but the broader record shows baggage changes with trip demands. Bulky conference materials and booth clothing make this closer to the gear-driven checked-bag cases than the light Minneapolis or Raleigh work setups.
probes.query: For a fresh solo conference trip to Las Vegas, I need a poster tube, handouts, and a suit for the booth. Pick the baggage plan.

choices.text: Book the closest museum hotel.
Book the official museum-area hotel.
Book the farther suite hotel with breakfast.
Book the boutique by the first museum.

probes.difficulty_rationale: No prices or walking times are given, and a no-car museum weekend makes proximity very plausible. The challenge is rejecting a fixed closest-hotel reading of the many work-trip proximity choices.
probes.gold_action: Book the farther suite hotel with breakfast.
probes.label_rationale: Family trips have favored room to spread out, breakfast, and easy evenings, as in D.C. and Boston. The close or official hotel wins in the record were tied to early starts, weather, or event logistics, which are weaker for midmorning museum entries.
probes.query: For a fresh Philadelphia family weekend, museum entries are midmorning, and we will not have a car. The options are a closest museum hotel with standard rooms, an official museum-area hotel, a suite hotel a few blocks farther with breakfast, and a boutique by the first museum. Pick the hotel.

choices.text: Book the Midtown suite hotel with breakfast.
Book the official venue hotel.
Book the hotel attached to the venue.
Book the standard room across from the venue.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Official, attached, and across-the-venue hotels all look reasonable for a work retreat. The prior proximity-heavy work cases make those distractors tempting without the full context-sensitive pattern.
probes.gold_action: Book the Midtown suite hotel with breakfast.
probes.label_rationale: The prior attached or official hotel choices were justified by early work starts, weather, and venue friction. Here the late start and family evenings make the suite-and-breakfast logic from D.C. and Boston more relevant than strict proximity.
probes.query: For a fresh Nashville work retreat, sessions start late morning, and my family joins for evenings. Options are the official venue hotel, a Midtown suite hotel with breakfast, a hotel attached to the venue, and a cheaper standard room across from the venue. Pick the hotel.

choices.text: Book the hotel closest to Pike Place.
Book the standard room beside the museum.
Book the hotel closest to the first activity.
Book the South Lake Union suite with breakfast.

probes.difficulty_rationale: With no car and sightseeing split across neighborhoods, the closest-location options remain attractive. The complete record is needed to keep proximity as a tradeoff rather than a fixed rule.
probes.gold_action: Book the South Lake Union suite with breakfast.
probes.label_rationale: Split family activities weaken a single closest-site answer, while room space, breakfast, and easy routines match the family hotel choices in D.C. and Boston. Prior proximity wins were for specific work-event risks, not for every trip.
probes.query: For a fresh Seattle family weekend, activities are split between Pike Place and the science museum, and there is no car. Options are a hotel closest to Pike Place, a standard room beside the museum, a hotel closest to the first activity, and a roomier South Lake Union suite with breakfast. Pick the hotel.
